subsubtopic: PROPOSED RELOCATION OF SASKATOON OFFICE-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a motion of urgent and pressing necessity. The Post Office is planning to move the Saskatchewan district office from Saskatoon to Winnipeg, leaving Saskatchewan and Prince Edward Island as the only two provinces without district offices.
In view of the fact that there are a substantially greater number of post offices in Saskatchewan than in Manitoba, spread over a far larger area, and the move will mean a loss of 103 positions with a salary of about $1% million per year to the city of Saskatoon alone, I move, and I should say that I had asked the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) to second this motion as he is the Liberal member twinned with Saskatoon East, but he demurred and it will therefore be seconded by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil):
That this House directs the Postmaster General, in the interests of efficiency of operation of the Post Office in western Canada, to revoke the plan to move the Saskatchewan district office from the city of Saskatoon to the city of Winnipeg.

subsubtopic: PROGRAM SET OUT IN NIAGARA FALLS "REVIEW"-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43. At this crucial moment in our history, all Canadians outside the province of Quebec find themselves at a loss as to how they, as individuals, can show to the people of Quebec in a tangible way their true feelings about Quebec, its culture, its language, its people and the fact that we in the rest of the country accept that a Canada without the beautiful province of Quebec is unthinkable.
All hon. members have been, or will be, supplied with a copy of the Niagara Falls Review of April 22 which sets forth a program for one-to-one communication between residents of Canada outside Quebec and residents within Quebec. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Guelph (Mr. Schroder):
That this House urge the press in every municipality outside the province of Quebec to forthwith establish a program similar to the one set out in the Niagara Falls Review of April 22, 1980, and that all Canadians outside Quebec be invited to take advantage of such programs to express to the people of Quebec their deep feelings of love and affection.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to introduce a motion dealing with an important matter of pressing necessity.
Considering that the western premiers have unanimously stated that they are in favour of renewing the constitution; considering that they emphatically reject sovereignty-association and the status quo; and considering the recent commitment made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in favour of a renewed federalism, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp):
That the House call on the Prime Minister of Canada to answer affirmatively to the wish expressed by his western counterparts.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. It relates to questions put to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) and answered by him today, arising out of his statement to the House yesterday on the tabling of the main estimates. If I may say so, it is rather fundamental that the minister indicated to the House yesterday that what he was tabling were estimates, and I quote him from page 290 of Hansard:
-without any changes to reflect the policies this government is in the process of elaborating.
The lead questions to him today were designed to find out exactly what he meant by that and whether there was any explanation that he had to give to indicate that, by adopting the procedure being proposed, we would be giving the government a blank cheque with respect to the main estimates and that we would have to wait for some future time with respect to its future expenditure plans.
Privilege-Mr. W. Baker
In the course of his statement yesterday, and he alluded to it again today, the minister indicated that there were several specific cases in which future supplementary estimates will reflect the changes in programs in these main estimates. He went on at that point to indicate that there was a $2.6 billion provision in the 1980-81 estimates for oil import compensation which was based on something that apparently is not akin or related to what the present government intends to do. He said they were reviewing the capital financing arrangements for Petro-Canada. He also said there were matters concerning the unemployment insurance program. Then he said this:
Madam Speaker, these are a few of the items which may have their main estimates funding level adjusted to reflect this government's policies and programs.
What he is really saying is that these main estimates in terms of the programs and policies of this government are absolutely meaningless. He is in effect asking Parliament to accept this process blindly. Frankly, I think it is a fetter on the rights of Parliament and the right of the public to know what the government intends to do. It is a trespassing on what I consider the legitimate concerns of members.
To cement it even further he went on to say, as reported at page 292:
They are being recommended for adoption subject to such modifications as may subsequently be made thereto through tabling supplementary estimates to give effect to policy changes which this administration may wish to introduce.
What the minister is really saying is that the consideration of the government's programs in these estimates in this House of Commons is meaningless. Frankly, 1 do not think we should put up with it. That is the position I take. It is about time the government realized that if there is a problem, it has to innovate some way to change it.
As reported at page 296 he said:
They do not represent an expenditure plan by this government.
Estimates are important to members of Parliament. They are either considered in this House in Committee of the Whole or in a standing committee of the House of Commons. It is only through consideration of the spending programs of the government that we can make an appropriate judgment with respect to the relevancy of those programs to the needs of Canadians. Indeed, it is the only way that members of Parliament can hold the government accountable for what it says to the Canadian people about what it intends to do.
In answer to the second question put by one of my colleagues, the minister indicated that it is always the objective of the government to fulfil this commitment with respect to maintaining a certain level of expenditures. That answer is quite different from one which he gave at the press conference. I quote from The Globe and Mail of April 23, 1980:
-Treasury Board president Donald Johnston admitted he could not predict when the Liberals might meet their election promise to hold down the annual increase in government spending to the nominal rate of increase in the gross national product.
That can have a dramatic effect on the deficit, on the administration of government programs, and on the delivery of government services to the people we represent. Quite frankly,

April 23, 1980
Privilege-Mr. W. Baker
I do not think this Parliament should be asked to deal with a meaningless blue book, a book of figures that, in terms of this government's policy and this government's expenditure plans and programs it says it wants to put forward, is absolutely meaningless.
I raise this because it is important for Parliament in the consideration of the estimates by Parliament. 1 raise it for the purpose of saying to the President of the Treasury Board and to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard), whom I deal with quite amicably, that it is important before we get into this too far that there be a statement made to catch up with what has been laid out in the estimates, i.e., the plans and programs. It is important. It will be against that program, that statement of expenditure plans that we will be able to make appropriate judgments as to the propriety of the government's programs. Those are judgments we want to make. Whether the government likes them or not is irrelevant.
1 raise this to give my friend, the President of the Treasury Board, an opportunity to consider a course of action which will allow him to give more precise answers to Parliament than the estimates which he tabled yesterday, and much more specific answers with respect to the questions put to him today. It is important to the people that the estimates process not be rendered meaningless and not be watered down like a number of other processes around here.

subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (NEPEAN-CARLETON)-TABLING OF MAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my hon. colleague has raised this issue as a question of privilege but I think it would have been more appropriate to have risen on a point of order. But if his purpose in rising was to make sure that the House will have the opportunity to study thoroughly both main estimates and the supplementary estimates, then I can reassure him immediately. We have had consultations together-he is aware of that- to ensure that the estimates of previous years can be reviewed by the opposition within reasonable and fair time, taking into account the two elections that took place in the last 12 months. I want to point out publicly to the House that we are prepared to allot the same period of time to the opposition parties as provided for under our Standing Orders, if these provisions could have been applied and if the estimates had been tabled on time last March 1. So I would like to give that assurance to the leaders and again to the House leader of the official opposition and 1 definitely see nothing wrong with what the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) did yesterday.
What the President of the Treasury Board did was to table the main estimates and he clearly said the following, as reported at page 292 of Hansard in response to a request for clarification made by the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), and I quote:
They are being tabled legally as our estimates but, as 1 indicated, we will be bringing forward supplementary estimates to give effect to those changes-
All these supplementary estimates, Madam Speaker, are subject to consideration by committees of the House. Yesterday, after the President of the Treasury Board had tabled supplementary estimates (A) in addition to the main estimates, I presented a motion to refer these supplementary estimates to the appropriate committees of members of both sides of the House so that there be an opportunity of scrutinizing them thoroughly. So in the procedure that has been followed everything is legal and in conformity with Standing Orders 58 and 59 which are the only ones applicable and pertinent and nothing irregular has resulted from the attitude and the approach taken by the President of the Treasury Board.
This being said, Madam Speaker, again I want to assure hon. members opposite that we on the government side intend to allow them at least as much time as that which is provided for under our Standing Orders for the main and supplementary estimates, just as if the main estimates had been tabled at the proper time. My hon. colleagues are aware that we are operating under exceptional circumstances, having had to go to the people twice within a year, which does not happen every day.
We are therefore faced with the following situation: the 1979-80 estimates have never been approved by the House, and what matters even more, the 1980-81 estimates were not tabled on March 1 last as they were supposed to be under our Standing Orders, and this, for reasons which are clear. And because the main estimates were not tabled on March 1, the normal time limits for the debate on these estimates which are set under our Standing Orders cannot apply, so that we are entirely at the mercy of the opposition which, in theory, could cause the debate to drag on for years, if it wanted to, and therefore prevent the government from dealing with both the main and supplementary estimates.
I know this is not the official opposition's nor the New Democratic Party's intention. There has been in our negotiations up till now a spirit of co-operation that leads us to be optimistic that an agreement can be reached to reinstate so to speak a procedure allowing for serious consideration both of these main estimates and supplementary estimates. No dilatory consideration of course, or one that would leave the feeling that the official opposition is acting irresponsibly. I am convinced on the contrary that the official opposition will act responsibly, it will not use this truly exceptional situation to prevent Parliament from operating normally and disposing of the legislative work accumulated as a result of two successive elections in a year, as called for by His Excellency the Governor General in the throne speech last week.
This being said, Madam Speaker, 1 give to my hon. colleague the assurance he will have at least as much time as that provided by the Standing Orders were they applicable. This indeed is the formula we are negotiating on, and on which I am expecting an understanding from my colleague within the next two days if at all possible.
April 23, 1980

So, we will allow ample time to the official opposition, and on the other hand, the procedure followed up till now and in the future will be strictly and absolutely consistent with Standing Orders 58 and 59, which are relevant in the matter.

subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (NEPEAN-CARLETON)-TABLING OF MAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the government House leader has addressed himself to some other question of privilege. He has not addressed himself to the question of privilege raised by the opposition House leader. It is not a question of how much time there is in which to study the estimates or of how much time the government House leader, in his generosity, is going to mete out to us. The question is, what are we going to study? Are we going to study estimates which the government is standing behind, or are we going to study estimates just thrown in to us like a dog to a bone, or a bone to a dog, so that we will be kept busy playing around and the government can get interim supply?
Neither the President of the Treasury Board nor the government has made it clear that these main estimates are anything but a fiction. Let me refer you, Madam Speaker, to the speech on Monday night by the effervescent Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) who is now effervescing in West Germany-I hope his message there is accepted in a better way than it was here the other night. This is what he said-1 am not referring to Hansard, 1 am referring to the prepared speech:
The information on the current 1980-81 fiscal outlook will serve as a supplement to the main estimates which are to be tabled tomorrow.
That is a piece of impertinence in itself, to suggest that a speech by him is going to be a supplement to the main estimates. He goes on to say that the main estimates are those prepared by the former government which were ready for printing when the present government took office. He tells us:
It was judged best not to attempt to revise this massive compilation of expenditure figures, but to table the existing material without delay-
Why, Madam Speaker? As a basis upon which interim supply could be sought. It was a frank admission that these estimates will be brought into the House in an attempt to get interim supply through, not as estimates for 1980-81 but just as something thrown as a bone to a dog so that we can chew on it and vote interim supply while the government carries on with the real estimates, whatever those estimates are.
He went on to say:
The expenditure figures in the fiscal forecast I am tabling are based upon the main estimates but contain, in addition,-
Then he gives his own estimates of what the outlays are likely to be. He disagrees totally with the outlays contained in these main estimates. Then, two pages further on, he says this-this is contempt. Madam Speaker; the man should be brought before the bar of this House in shackles:
I would further like it to be understood, however, that these projections do not in any way constitute the expenditure plan or the planned financial requirements of this government for fiscal year 1980-81.
Privilege-Mr. W. Baker
He wants us to understand that these estimates, his projections, are not in any way the expenditure plan or the planned financial requirements of the government. One loses one breath at the audacity of it. These estimates are tabled and we are baldfacedly told that they do not contain the expenditure plan for the projected financial requirements of the government. Surely we have the right to ask what are the planned financial requirements for the government, and what is the expenditure plan.
If the government is not recommending these estimates except in a technical sense, what are its estimates, and should this House accept estimates-they were tabled as main estimates-that two ministers frankly tell the House are not the estimates they are going to go by? We are being asked to vote money that the government is telling us in advance it is not going to spend in accordance with how we voted. Ministers are going to spend the money just as they feel they want to spend it, with no further reference to this House until they come back with supplementary estimates later in the year or next year. The bald-faced effrontery of those statements demands that this chamber rise up on its hind legs and say, "This is enough; we are not going to vote main estimates which ministers tell us do not constitute their expenditure plan, do not constitute their planned financial requirements". In other words, it is a piece of fiction which they are putting before us to get interim supply-not likely-and then ask us to co-operate in doing it.
So, Madam Speaker, if you look at what is said by the Minister of Finance and what was confirmed yesterday by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston), he could not be forced into an admission that he supported these estimates. He gave all kinds of examples of where they are going to change the estimates. In fact, they already had them changed before he tabled them. We do not know what authority he had for any of that. I do not want to give the quotations that my hon. friend has already given, but there is another quotation or two that I want to give. He could not give us answers, of course, in any event, on some of the questions that we asked him. I think that the quotations 1 am looking for have already been given, so I do not want to repeat that, but when he was questioned by the hon. member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty), he would not say that they were putting these expenditure plans forward or that-oh, here it is. Page 292:
They are being recommended for adoption subject to such modifications as may subsequently be made thereto through tabling supplementary estimates to give effect to policy changes which this administration may wish to introduce.
1 say fine, Madam Speaker. If there are policy changes not now decided upon that occur later in the year, which the government cannot foresee, then that is a proper use of supplementary estimates. They come in with supplementary estimates. They say to the House of Commons, "Sorry, members of the House of Commons and the Senate, we did not know when we put the main estimates before you that certain events were going to happen. There was a catastrophe. We did

April 23, 1980
Privilege-Mr. W. Baker
not know we had to spend money. There was a flood here, there was something unexpected there, or there is a massive change in policy on, say, the oil import subsidy program", or whatever the policy is, "and therefore we now have to ask you for forgiveness and to give us supplementary estimates". That is the procedure. You do not come in with the main estimates and say, "Disregard these main estimates; they are going to be whatever we say they are when the time comes that we feel suited to tell you what they are".
So, Madam Speaker, this is in line with the point of privilege that was before you yesterday. Because this government has a majority, it thinks it can do exactly what it likes, and what it now wants to do is to have this huge blue book referred to all the House standing committees and get all the backbenchers and members on this side busy examining the estimates and questioning the officials. Then the lordly ministers will come down every once in a while with their satraps around them or whatever, the flapdoodlers. They are experts. They will come in, the swarms, like they are going to the hive. They are honey bees, queen bees. The swarms of advisers will come down occasionally. We will spend all our time questioning them on these estimates, and after we are through with all that and report back and they are passed by the House, while this is going on they are back in their offices changing the estimates all around because these are not their main estimates.
So what is the point of our having these estimates referred at all to any of these committees? The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance is one of the worst offenders. He is already busy changing these estimates, and his minister has admitted it, so for them to come before this House in this disgraceful manner-it was not bad enough that they disrupted and ruptured the whole budgetary process; they are now gouging the whole system of considering estimates, and we have to appeal to you, Madam Speaker, for protection and to put a stop to this.
When the House leader goes on about how much time he is going to give, we want time to consider real estimates. We do not want time to consider fictional estimates. We want time to consider the government's real spending plans. That is what we want the time for.
Just look at the outrageous speech of the Minister of Finance, who has gone off now ringing the gong in Munich, or whatever he is doing in Munich. I hope it is only a gong he is ringing. He said that he wants us to understand that the projections do not in any way constitute the expenditure plan or the planned financial requirements of this government. "Do not in any way", Madam Speaker. Well, of all the brazen effrontery that has ever been put before a House of Commons, that takes the cake, and that is why we bring up this point of privilege, and that is why we ask you. Madam Speaker, to consider this, as I know you will, extremely seriously with the other piece, the other-for whom the bell tolls. The bell is tolling for this House of Commons in this session and in the next four years, because already in the House we are here only
six days and two of our cherished traditions have been done away with.

subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (NEPEAN-CARLETON)-TABLING OF MAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would have deferred to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston), but I want to say a few words in support of the position taken by my two colleagues.
There is no more fundamental right and responsibility of Parliament than control of the public purse. This very institution developed because of a concern among the people of Britain that proper control over the public purse was not being exercised. This is the central function which we, as parliamentarians, are asked to discharge as part of our responsibilities.
What the government has done by putting forward estimates that it will not stand behind, and which it disavowed any responsibility for at the very time they were tabled, has been to make a mockery of our attempts to discharge our responsibilities on behalf of our constituents. What happened yesterday when the President of the Treasury Board tabled the 1980-81 estimates was that he not only denied paternity but also disinherited the child at the same time. He said in the course of his remarks that there were going to be substantial changes made. He made it very clear that these estimates did not constitute the spending plan of this government. My colleagues have quoted that statement on his part.
Madam Speaker, if you take a look at Hansard pages 290 and 291 yesterday, you will find that fully one-half of the minister's remarks were designed to indicate changes that he intended to make from these estimates and to indicate why these estimates did not represent the spending intentions of the government. He concluded that section by saying, and I quote:
Madam Speaker, there are a few of the items which may have their main estimates funding level adjusted to reflect this government's policies and programs.
Clearly, the implication of that is that this is only a portion of the changes, and that what Parliament knows about today when it is asked to approve this blue book of estimates is only a portion of the changes which this government intends to make. So I ask you, Madam Speaker, how can we be called upon to discharge our responsibility to guard the public purse when the estimates which are being presented to us are patently phony, even on the basis of the testimony of the minister who introduces them?
When I tried to question the President of the Treasury Board to ask him what the spending plans of the government are-because this is central at the time we are approving the estimates; what else are the estimates for?-his response today was to refer me to the statement by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) two days ago. Well, in that statement the Minister of Finance expressly said that that statement did not constitute the spending plans of the government either.
The central question here is, what are the estimates? What is the purpose of estimates? If we cannot get the spending plans of the government from the estimates, where does Parliament get them? What is our job? What is our responsibility? What is the point of these estimates we are being asked to
April 23, 1980

approve? What does the government intend to do with the money we approve if we go ahead on the basis of these estimates which hon. members opposite themselves say are false and do not represent their spending plans?
The issue which my colleague, the Elouse leader, was raising, was not that which was raised by the government House leader, a question of how much time we would have to examine these estimates. We want adequate time, but the central question is this: are the documents being put before the House? Is the recommendation coming at the request of the President of the Treasury Board for the appropriation of funds meaningful, or are we being asked to appropriate funds for programs which this government already has no intention of carrying out?
1 submit that unless there is some candour shown by the government very soon in terms of indicating what its full spending plans are and in terms of setting for us a target for its spending for this year-because that is what the estimates are designed to do-if the government does not do that, Parliament is rendered meaningless and irrelevant, and there is no way we can continue to consider estimates which, on the testimony of the minister presenting them, are false.
That is the central issue here, and it is one to which the President of the treasury board has the responsibility to address himself. When will he be candid with this Parliament? When will he table the government's spending plan? When will he in fact give us the information that is essential before we are asked to approve one penny of the spending estimates which are before us today?
These estimates would have been relevant if the budget of the former minister of finance had been passed on December 13, instead of being defeated. If we had not had an election on February 18, these estimates would have been relevant. But all of that has happened, and this government indicates that it does not stand by these estimates, that they do not represent its spending plans, which means then that before ministers ask us to appropriate the funds for which they are asking they have a responsibility to level with the Canadian people and with Parliament, and say what in fact their spending plans are. That they have not done, Madam Speaker.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (NEPEAN-CARLETON)-TABLING OF MAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I find that this whole performance by my friends in the opposition to be quite extraordinary. This righteous indignation is coming from the hon. members who last year retabled the estimates which had been tabled by the Liberal administration in the spring-they retabled them in the autumn. I do not have the specific statement made by the then president of the treasury board in front of me, but my recollection is that all he said was that he was tabling these estimates and that he had no comment to make.
When I tabled the estimates yesterday, I said that we were recommending their adoption, subject to certain changes, and 1 tried to give the opposition every indication of which way we would be moving.
These estimates are not at all irrelevant. I realize that the gentlemen opposite were not in government for any great
Privilege-Mr. W. Baker
length of time, nor have 1 been, but at leat 1 know that the process of developing main estimates is one which extends over even more than one year. So it is perfectly obvious that these estimates have validity and that they should be adopted subject to the kind of modifications which we will be bringing forward.
When the hon. member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty) says to us that these estimates would have been relevant had the budget put forward by the former minister of finance been adopted, 1 say to you. Madam Speaker, that that is an interesting observation because a number of events have taken place since that night in December which would have made these main estimates, in their view, also outdated and outmoded, for several reasons.
First of all, as I think 1 indicated earlier, subsequent to the budget address there was an oil price increase. The oil price increase wiped out the so-called reserve to which reference was made by the former president of the Treasury Board yesterday, and, accordingly, the $58.4 billion projection-which was a projection and did not represent the estimates-became irrelevant. Subsequently they would have been faced with further oil price increases and public debt charge increases, and all of these would have had to be taken into account in the very hypothetical situation of their having been returned to power. It would have been necessary for them to bring forward supplementary estimates at the time of tabling the main estimates, and it would have been necessary for them to bring forward supplementary estimates during the course of the year.
In fact, it seems to me that we have been particularly candid in indicating in the message which 1 delivered yesterday, in my capacity as President of the Treasury Board, the specific areas in which we would hope to make particular and important policy decisions and changes. The guaranteed income supplement is one, and hon. members opposite are fully aware of it.
I must say that I find this performance extraordinary, in light of their own established precedents last year and in light of the fact that this government was elected on February 18 and we have already tabled these estimates. Obviously we have had no opportunity to make technical amendments to estimates of this size and complexity which have been developed over a multi-month period. I find no basis for the seeking of privilege, or for their protest, or for whatever comes forward from my hon. friends opposite. It seems to me that we have been candid. We have given a full explanation, we have tabled the estimates in a timely manner, and, as the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) has indicated, opposition members will have ample time to consider these estimates in committee. The President of the Privy Council has given that commitment to the opposition.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

plans of the previous government. The plans the present President of the Treasury Board tabled in the House yesterday are not, on the admission of both the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) in his speech, and of the President of the Treasury Board, the spending plans of this government. subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (NEPEAN-CARLETON)-TABLING OF MAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have just a comment on this matter. It is a pretty serious matter that this House is being asked to consider, followed by committee consideration. We are already asked to consider something that will not in fact be the spending plans of the government. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston), however, says that there will be minor alterations. Therefore, it should be possible for him, I expect, to table immediately amendments, or an addendum to his tabling yesterday of the blue book, indicating the alterations.
1 can understand why he would not want to go through the problems of printing and segregating by page and reference number the details in that monster telephone book we call the blue book, but surely it would be possible for him to provide us with an addendum, not a supplement, so that we could really see what the spending plans of this government are. If they are what he says they are, that is, only minor alterations, small changes in interest expense of a billion dollars or so, small changes in the cost of oil subsidy of maybe a couple of billion dollars, then it should be possible for him surely to table addenda to this blue book so that the committees of the House can study the estimates properly and know what the spending plans of the government are. But he does not seem to want to do that. He says that here is something that was prepared back in December, that it does not mean anything, that they are not going to follow it, that they have changed their direction, that they defeated the budget of December 11.
The President of the Treasury Board says he does not stand behind the estimates completely and that they are subject to change. If they are subject to change, and if he wants the House to study them here and in committee, if he does not want to waste the time of members of Parliament, and if he wants to treat Parliament honestly, then surely he will come clean with Parliament and, before these estimates go to the committee, he will give us an addendum to them. The tabling he did yesterday is clearly wrong. I cannot see how members of Parliament can be asked to study something that the government itself says is wrong. If the government says that it is wrong, then the government should point out the corrections. Clearly there will be changes.
These estimates were prepared in December, and there has been an election in the interval. The government has clearly indicated a totally new direction for Canada. The spending that Parliament is being asked to approve on that new direction for Canada, surely should be reflected in the changes filed with the work that was done last fall. We appreciate the problem in preparing estimates. We are not trying to hold the House up; we are not trying to hold the government up. But we want some honesty from them, just some simple honesty. As members of Parliament, we will have to study the estimates. Surely we want to study what the government really intends to spend.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I apologize for my tardiness in that I did not rise to my feet. It is one of those afternoons, but 1 thank other hon. members of the House for their agreement to move this particular measure along with some dispatch. While it is simple in its purpose and intent, it is very urgent in its result and consequence. Bill C-2 is something which has been required for a long time and without its passage it would result in very severe consequences for the refugee program in this country.
Simply what the bill intends to do is to raise the loans ceiling in the immigration loans fund from the present level of $20 million to $60 million. As members will know, the loans fund goes back a long time in terms of the immigration programs of this country, back to about 1951. The basic principle of it is that the Government of Canada sets up a revolving loans fund and advances moneys to refugees and

April 23, 1980
Immigration Act
immigrants coming to this country to help pay for their transportation, and those funds are then repaid.
I am pleased to report to the House that over that period the return and repayment factor has been exceedingly high, somewhere in the neighbourhood of 95 per cent. Thus, the revolving loans fund has proven its validity and its soundness as a financial measure, and carries with it very little extra cost to the government. The only extra cost is encountered in terms of the actual money that we borrow to advance to refugees, which is lent to them at no cost during the time of repayment. But 1 would hasten to add that the repayment is exceedingly quick and that the turn around time is very little time at all.
1 would like to illustrate that by the example of a letter I received from Mr. John Derkson, who is a representative of the Mennonite Brethren in my own province of Manitoba, and who has been very active in the sponsorship of refugees. He sent me a note with a letter he received from one of the refugees who had received a loan from our fund, and pointed out that in a mere four months from his arrival in Canada that particular refugee had paid back the entire sum of the $750 loan we advanced him. That is only illustrative of the general pattern of responsibility and obligation that those who receive loans from this fund have shown.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO INCREASE LOANS TO IMMIGRANTS

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO INCREASE LOANS TO IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:
It just happens to be in my constituency, as the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) illustrates.
We have to increase the ceiling at this point in time, Mr. Speaker, because of the substantial numbers of additional refugees who have been brought into this country since 1979. In saying that I would pay some tribute to my predecessor who did initiate the refugee program in 1979 and was able to establish the program of matching grants to induce and provide a strong incentive for a very large contribution by the private, voluntary sector in this country. In fact I would say that what we have witnessed in Canada over the past years, in terms of the enormous outpouring of generosity by private Canadians through church organizations and voluntary organizations, is one of the great success stories in this country.
The reason we have added to those numbers is just to go back to the original formula established by my predecessor, where there would be some degree of equity or matching between government and private sponsors. It is our feeling that we want to encourage the continuation of that kind of generosity and contribution the private sector, or the volunteer sector, has been giving us in helping us deal with the very vast and major refugee problems which will continue to plague this world, and in respect of which our own country can be of major assistance.
As a consequence of those additional 60,000 refugees coming from South Vietnam, obviously the loan fund was over-extended. For the past several months in order to maintain the program, during the time of dissolution, the election, and delay in Parliament being called, the program has had to
be operated under the requirement of warrants by the government. Because Parliament is now sitting, the time within which we can ask for a warrant will expire sometime in early May. Therefore I want to point out to members the urgency of moving this bill through as quickly as possible.
If we are not able to pass it and raise the ceiling in order to bring the loan fund up to its proper maximum, this would mean substantial cancellation of the airlift that is presently going on. It would mean we would have to break many commitments with the chartered airlines, and it would mean that the entire refugee program would be severely disrupted over that period of time, and would not provide the continuity that is required. What that does in terms of damaging our reputation internationally is obvious. I think far more severe is what it does in terms of the opportunity to provide continued placement of refugees in this country. Therefore I would say it is very important for this House to treat the matter with expedition and dispatch.
I would say to those members in this House who want to use this as an opportunity to raise greater questions about the direction and thrust of refugee programs and immigration policy, I personally welcome that kind of contribution, and it has certainly been my intention, and the intention of the government, to review the over-all question of refugee programs. I hope to come to grips with a larger and more comprehensive commitment so that we will not simply be forced into ad hoc responses year after year. This is something that will provide a program that will incorporate the newfound contribution of the voluntary sector with our own efforts as a government. I would hope that any comments of that kind could be restrained and perhaps restricted until another time, certainly on estimates or when we make statements in the House, because I think the urgency of getting this bill through is so great that such a debate, which I would welcome and in fact invite, might be delayed until a somewhat later date. In saying that, I will follow my own advice and recommend this measure to the House. It is an important measure, its urgency is great, and I hope that we will be able to dispatch it within this day's sitting.

speechtext:
Thank you, very much, Mr. Speaker, for recognizing me.
There has not been a large measure of agreement throughout this session, at least from where I sit, but I suggest that this is one of those occasions when we are happy to co-operate with what the minister suggests in terms of the urgency of this bill and the appropriateness of it, in terms of it being a constructive measure.
May I say that many of the assertions made by the minister are in fact correct. The loan program has been a constructive and useful vehicle. We know there has been repayment on a prompt basis, and the statistics, as I understand them, show almost 95 per cent in terms of repayment.
1 also point out that it is necessary, in terms of the expenses which have increased dramatically since the last time, to support it. The summation of what I am really saying is that we constructively support this bill.
April 23, 1980

I will be reasonably brief, but there are a couple of comments 1 would like to make about immigration and immigration policy generally. Immigration policy, and especially the levels of immigration into Canada, represent one of the most sensitive and important social issues that this House will have to face. It is important, as with any issue, that we understand what are the facts. Before we can come to any type of reasoned conclusion, it is important that we all take the time to ascertain what are the correct facts.
Many people in Canada, and many people in this House, would be surprised to know that in 1978 net immigration into Canada was less than 15,000 people. I myself found that astonishing, and people I have spoken to since have found that to be astonishing. This is something I think many people should understand.
The second thing 1 should like to point out to other members in this House has regard to the fact that we should have some sense of realism as to the capacity of the country to absorb the numbers of people who come into the country. The refugee program, which I am happy to say my predecessor implemented, is an imaginative program. It is a program that brought a spirit of generosity to it. It is a program that I wholly support and endorse. I do point out and caution that, no matter what good will exists within this House, there have to be certain realistic limitations as to what this country can absorb. I think there will be a day when we can debate exactly what those limits are.
The final matter I should like to bring to the attention of this House is contained in the annual report to Parliament for 1980, which was tabled in November of last year. On reading the levels of immigration, in particular at page 28, I was somewhat amazed to find that between 1974 and 1978 the family class category of admission of immigrants had risen from 24.8 per cent to 53.5 per cent. Over that same period the independent category of people had dropped from 50.8 per cent to 25.6 per cent. There is no doubt that in certain of the western provinces there is a need for skilled people. I hope that at some point in time we will have an opportunity to debate whether the program should be more balanced. We should have an opportunity to discuss whether we should have more independent people who have trades and come in by merit, or at least reassess the balance in respect of the family category.
I know there is some urgency in getting this matter through, and in the interest of brevity I will conclude my remarks. Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO INCREASE LOANS TO IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on behalf of my party to support the principles enunciated in this bill. My party has done so on each occasion such a bill has been brought forward.
I have been looking at the record of Canada in the area of immigration. It is a record which, I believe, cannot be matched by any of the other industrialized countries of the world. Since the end of the World War II, over 4.5 million people have come to Canada as immigrants or refugees. I am happy with
Immigration Act
that fact and the fact that, unlike the period just before and just after World War II, the immigrants who have come to Canada have not only been from northern Europe and western Europe, but from all parts of the world, areas such as southern Europe, Africa, Asia, the West Indies, and South America. They are not just people who are white Anglo-Saxon protestants, but people from all races and of all religions.
My party is also proud of the fact that in every one of the recent crises in which refugees have been driven from their countries, whether it was Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Poland, Uganda, Chile or, as it has been for the last couple of years, from the Indo-Chinese countries, Canada has been in the forefront in accepting and in willingness to accept these refugees.
I do not wish to prolong the debate, but my party is happy with the fact that the Immigration Act which we now have recognized refugees as an admissible category, that procedures have been established for the selection of refugees abroad, and that there is a procedure in Canada for applying for refugee status. These applications are now considered by the Refugee Status Advisory Committee. We are also happy with the fact that Canada has ratified the United Nations Convention on Refugees. We are not happy with the fact that we have not incorporated all of the provisions of that convention in our own legislation. My party believes that the time has come for Canada to reconcile our acceptance of the UN convention with our laws and regulations with regard to immigration.
We approve of this bill because, as the minister has said, there are a large number of refugees who have come to Canada, and more who will be coming, and because money is needed to help these people resettle. We join with the minister and with the official opposition in expressing our satisfaction with the way in which the refugees and immigrants have been fitted into this country once they have arrived. This has been demonstrated to a large extent by the number of these people, 95 per cent or more, who have repaid the loans advanced to them to assist them in resettling in Canada.
Having said that, I would like to say to the minister, as I said on the occasion a bill of this type was last debated in 1967 and on other occasions, that I think it is time that we look at the practical problems which we face in Canada, partly as a result of our constitution. It is the federal government-this minister and his department-which decides how many people will be allowed into Canada, from where they will come, and who will come.
As I look at the immigration figures, I cannot help but be amazed at the wide fluctuations between them. Let me give a few illustrations to indicate what has happened. In 1967
222,000	people were permitted to come into Canada. Just three years later in 1970 that figure dropped to 147,000 people. Then in 1974 it went up to 218,000 people, and in 1978 the figure was down again to 86,000 people. The hon. member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer) put the number much lower. He must have deducted the people who left the country from the people who came into the country.

April 23, 1980
Immigration Act
These figures denote a very pragmatic policy, and that is putting it nicely. It certainly does not indicate that we have made much progress toward a well thought out consistent policy to which we could adhere from year to year. I recognize that the question of immigration and of permitting refugees to enter this country is a very sensitive question and brings out very conflicting emotions. On the one hand there are people who have arrived fairly recently and who still have friends and relatives in the countries from which they came. Naturally, they want their friends and relatives to come to this country.
On the other hand, there are many people in this country whose parents, grandparents or great grandparents may indeed have been immigrants to this country, but they are now looking at the one million people who are unemployed and saying to their members of Parliament that we ought to go slow on the number of immigrants we permit to enter the country. As long as we have that kind of unemployment, it will be difficult to get a real consensus on this question. 1 suggest to the minister that in order to develop a policy which will meet with the approval of a very substantial majority of Canadians, we must move away from the kind of economic situation which we are in now with one million people unemployed.
1 would like to deal with one specific point before 1 sit down, and that is with regard to the problem of the federal government being in control of deciding how many people will come to Canada. The federal government also decides what countries these people will come from, but I do not disagree with that. 1 am very happy with the fact that so many of the immigrants in recent years have come from countries in which the official languages were not either English or French, the official languages of Canada.
Once these people get to Canada, and because education is the responsibility of the provinces, the federal government to a large extent forgets about these people. This, I feel, is a serious defect in our system. I say this because people who cannot speak the language will not only find it difficult, if not impossible, to obtain jobs, but will find it difficult to live in Canada except in a very closed society.
The minister grew up in the part of Winnipeg which 1 represent, and I am certain that he is not surprised when I say that I still meet people, particularly women, in their sixties and seventies, who have been in Canada for 30, 40 or 50 years and who still cannot speak English. Even if they can speak a little English, they are not comfortable with the language. These people came to Canada at a time when their husbands worked 60, 70 and even 80 hours a week. As a result, they have lived in their little communities and have not become familiar with the language.
Canada has done better in this area in recent years than it did 40 or 50 years ago. We now have programs which encourage people to learn the language and to learn a great deal more about Canada. However, these programs are far from covering all the needs.
On Monday of this week the Ottawa Citizen published a story headed, "Boat People Strive to Overcome Aches". The story goes on to say:
Their tales vary from loneliness and discouragement to pride and achievement.
For a handful of the Vietnamese boat people, the burdens of settling into the Canadian lifestyle have resulted in bouts of alcoholism and in a few cases, wife-beating.
But most of them agree with social agencies that their key frustrations are learning English or French, finding a job to support their families-
I know that there are programs and that the federal government pays for a certain number of people to take courses in a second language, either English or French, but the numbers for which the federal government pays are far short of the numbers who wish to take these courses. This is particularly true of married women who are not going out to find jobs and who are staying home. 1 say this is a very serious matter. Morally we have no right to put that burden on the provincial governments or on the municipalities.
Some years ago, 1 believe back in 1967 when we were discussing this matter, 1 pointed out that the city of Toronto estimated that it would cost that city $1.5 million a year to provide programs to educate the children in the Toronto schools who did not speak English at home. But now more than 50 per cent of the students attending schools in Toronto come from immigrant families where the language at home is not English. This has created tremendous problems in Toronto.
In my own city of Winnipeg-as I am sure the minister knows-where we have not experienced the number of immigrants as have cities such as Vancouver and Toronto, there are many classes in the core area where the majority of students are either from immigrant families or native families who do not speak English at home. This is a very serious problem for the people of Winnipeg as it is for the people in every city where this situation arises. 1 do not want to prolong the debate, Mr. Speaker, but I do want the minister to take note that at the appropriate time we certainly do intend to pursue this and other questions which we feel are very important if we are to look forward to a time when immigrants who have come to Canada will be able to fit into our society and play their full role.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO INCREASE LOANS TO IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief because 1 know we all want to have this bill passed quickly this afternoon. However, I would like to make one or two points because it is our first opportunity in some time to discuss a few immigration questions that have been building up because of some steps that have been taken resulting from the green paper discussion of a few years ago, and resulting from the long and interesting hearings that went on regarding the new Immigration Act.
First, I think we all agree with Bill C-2, and the question of raising the limits for assistance to refugees is something that we all support. I publicly supported the previous government's program last year when it was first introduced. My position has not changed since. I think the program to bring in the southeast Asian refugees was consistent with Canada's approach to refugee problems. There will be more and more
April 23, 1980

refugees in this era of world conflict in which we live, and 1 hope that the present government will be generous in its assistance to future refugee movements.
I believe it was this week when the minister announced that he was bringing in some of the people from the Peruvian embassy in Havana. I think he should be congratulated for that move.
On the broader question of our immigration policy, and the point raised by the hon. member who spoke a few moments ago, we learned at the committee hearings in the fall that the net intake of immigrants into Canada in the past 12 months was less than 15,000 people. Those of us who learned about that when the figure was made public in the fall were shocked.
Members of the House should again question a system that, in my view, has become so inflexible that it is impeding the growth of this country. I do not think a net intake of immigrants into Canada of 15,000 is enough to keep this country growing.
In my own area, the inner city of Toronto, 1 have noticed the effects the halt on immigration is having on small businesses, on the construction industry, on the appliance industry, and on all of the manufacturing jobs that were doing very well in the sixties and the early part of the seventies. I think it can be argued that the reduction in some of these areas is directly due to the fact that we now have such a small movement of immigrants into Canada. In my view, it is having grave consequences to large elements of our manufacturing sector.
I know that we do not want to go on too long this afternoon, but I am using this opportunity to flag a few of the things that I think we should be looking at as this Parliament progresses.
The hon. member who spoke earlier mentioned that the independent class over the past few years has become smaller in proportion to the family class. Certainly in the evidence that was presented to the various committees during our hearings, it was clear that people in the Department of Immigration were very concerned about it. Personally 1 think that we have to remember that members of the family class who come to Canada have to comply with occupational demand requirements. I think we tend to forget that. A person cannot come to Canada unless that person is a direct member of the immediate family, unless that person complies with occupational demand requirements. The problem has been that the occupational demand requirements are very stiff and inflexible.
The occupational and area demand report, that 1 believe is published four times a year by the department, say-for those who may have forgotten or who are not aware-that no matter what you do, what qualifications you have, or no matter what kind of contribution you can make in terms of being an industrious person who has abilities, if your particular occupation is rated zero, on a scale from zero to 15 in occupational demand in Canada, you are automatically excluded. That is the reason we have had only a net immigration flow into Canada of less than 15,000 people. 1 suspect that most members of this House would never be able to come into Canada under the current immigration requirements, in fact I doubt if
Immigration Act
5 per cent of members of the House of Commons would be allowed into Canada as landed immigrants under the current regulations.
In the search for a system we have effectively stopped the kinds of people who traditionally made the immigrant movement into Canada-enterprising people, people with a sense of adventure who always came to Canada because they were fed up with where they were. They had something to offer but they did not know what. They just set out, and by the millions made good in Canada. They contributed to the Canadian life and in a major way to the Canadian economy. We have now said to those people,"Stay home, you cannot come to Canada." That has very serious implications.
The attitude is all very well if someone says that because we have unemployment in Canada, we cannot bring in more people. However, the problem with that argument is that it does not point out that many of the people who are employing Canadians are people who were immigrants. They create jobs. The argument should be made that they create more jobs than they take away from Canadians and others in this country.
The system has to be reviewed. It has gone much too far in restricting the movement of enterprising people into Canada. In fact it has not only restricted but stopped it. It has made it zero. The large immigrant movement into Canada in the seventies has resulted in a tremendous contribution to the Canadian economy. We have now put a stop to that. I hope that hon. members, the minister and the officials will take note, look into this question, and use a little more common sense than saying to those who would make good Canadians, with their initiative and sense of adventure, that we do not want them. I do not think that is very good.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO INCREASE LOANS TO IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the use of funds loaned to people who are immigrants into Canada, whether they are independent immigrants-and I have had instances of loans in those cases-or whether they are refugees, has been a good investment for Canada. It is the kind of thing that Canada has done for a long time. Away back in pioneer days immigrants to this country were given assistance by our government, sometimes in terms of just a cow or a horse or some farm equipment. Helping a person to come to this country is important. The history of these loans has been that the vast majority of them have been instantly repaid. Therefore this has been a first class program, and the extension of it to $60 million is very appropriate.
The bill before us gives us an opportunity that we have not had for some time, namely, to say a few words with respect to immigration. It is important for members of Parliament. Mississauga is a city that has a great number of people who were born in other countries. Indeed, our city probably has people from every land in the world, not just nominal representatives but great numbers of people with different ethnic origins, cultures, and backgrounds. Therefore the whole question of immigration and how it is handled is important to the people of my city.

April 23, 1980
Immigration Act
The community dialogue that I sent to my constituents last March dealt entirely with immigration. As the replies to this questionnaire are received, 1 will be sending the material to the minister. I thought that today I would give the minister what we found in an analysis of the first 1,000 replies to that questionnaire, some of the problems raised by my constituents, and some of their attitudes.
It is important that we look at the question of immigration. How this or any other government handles immigration must depend on the feelings of those already here, particularly the feelings of those in a riding that is very much made up of immigrants. Their feelings and how they feel about further immigrants are something that must be considered in handling the whole matter of immigration into Canada.
Something 1 find very difficult is the fact that people somehow feel that their member of Parliament has great influence with the immigration minister. Indeed, last Saturday alone three sets of constituents came to see me on immigration matters. I do not think a week goes by that 1 do not write a letter to the minister. My executive assistant is probably on the phone to our immigration offices almost daily. Therefore this whole problem has to be resolved.
Some things must be done within the ministry. Some things should be done about the way it handles the over-all quota system required under the act. We should try to change the attitude of subjectiveness held by some people. My constituents firmly believe that the immigration officer who made the decision either liked them, did not like them, somebody had pull, somebody had drag, or that I, as a member of Parliament, could do something about it. I can assure them all 1 like. I certainly assured them in my newsletter that a member of Parliament might be able to tell them what the law is and to some extent the occupational demand and so on, but there is really not much I can do with respect to determining their points under the point system. Nonetheless the feeling persists, particularly for people who wish to bring their relatives to Canada.
The reason the number of family sponsored immigrants is up so dramatically is that the young, aggressive person wanting to come here as an independent may be turned down, but when it is a family matter, the family here and the immigrant in the other country keep pressing and eventually figure out how to accumulate the magic number of points in order to come here. It may well be the persistence of family sponsored immigrants that led to the situation where in 1978, 74.3 per cent of the immigrants were family sponsored whereas only 25.6 per cent were independent immigrants.
1 agree with the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery) that the independent immigrant who comes here to create and build in Canada, who has the pioneering instinct to come out on his own, is probably the kind of immigrant that will create a new industry and new opportunity for Canadians. That type of immigrant may not come in with the exact occupational skills we want, but his entrepreneurial abilities would go a long way toward creating jobs in this country.
There is another matter that must be brought to the attention of the minister. I am sure he knows about this because I wrote to him only yesterday. I refer to the way certain immigration offices throughout the world operate. I may be telling tales out of school about key immigration officials from the Toronto area, particularly Mississauga, but I am told, and I know from my own experience, that if you have a problem with the office in New Delhi or with the office in Port of Spain, forget it, because even telexes sent from the ministry itself to the ministry's own offices do not get answered. People can wait to be interviewed for two and three years; they will get no response to letters written, and clearly this creates social problems.
I am going to get into the question of ethnic origin and all the rest of it because I believe we have to pay attention to what people think. It may well be there is a hidden or isolated quota system in each office around the world and that the way to enforce a quota system is through bureaucratic delay. If that is the case, it is totally reprehensible. I have discussed this matter with all sorts of immigrant groups and it would not be reprehensible to them if they were to know in advance that the quota for the New Delhi office was 1,000 or 2,000, or whatever it was, and that once that office had accepted that number of people, no matter how it was arrived at, whether they were family sponsored or whatever, that office had fulfilled its function for the year and if you wanted to apply you had to wait until the following year or until there was a quota open for that office.
The global quota which, this year, is 120,000, seems like a lot, but in fact it may not be that many. It seems there is a tendency among our people, the constituents I represent-and I am speaking today almost entirely on behalf of my constituents, and I am not necessarily giving all of my own views, although some of mine are certainly included-to feel that certain offices are being used to ration, if you like, the Third World people who want to come here.
Getting into the question of ethnic origins, I did ask these questions in the questionnaire and I think the minister would be interested in the answers. I think we should look into the balance of how our population is made up. That is the kind of response I have received from people from China, from Kampuchea, from India, Pakistan, Uganda and so on. They say the same thing: we have got to keep some sort of balance in the country. That is not a racist remark; it is a question of how they have perceived the country to be made up. I think the minister should seriously consider publishing a breakdown of his quota, allowing certain percentages for each office so that people may know where they can apply and, if they have to come from one part of the world to that office. It certainly would lessen the difficulties encountered by members of Parliament in trying to get an answer out of an office which does not seem to want to reply.
Dealing with the criteria the minister follows at the present time under the act, there seem to be basically three criteria.

mmi
April 23, 1980

One, of course, is family unification. A second would be manpower needs in Canada and then, as the minister is aware, there is special provision for refugees, the ones we are taking from the Vietnam area and certain refugees from certain countries in Latin America plus self-exiled people who happen to come here from one of the communist countries. I sent all those details out to my constituents and received some interesting replies.
First of all, people in urban Canada have a perception that there are too many people coming into the country. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer), maybe there are a lot coming in but there are a lot going out. The net result, as was pointed out, was only 15,000 this year. When I asked my constituents whether they thought 120,000 was too high or too low or just about right, 13 per cent of them said it was too low, 25 per cent said it was about right, and 62 per cent said it was too high. That may be a question of communication by the department because as was pointed out by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) it may be that the perception that immigration is too high may be a bad communication problem by the ministry and by those involved in immigration, by those looking at the demographic requirements of Canada.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Cambridge, the net figure may be ridiculously low. Nonetheless, the percentage by people in Mississaugua is on those lines. No less than 62 per cent say that the figure of 120,000 allowed in under the present quota is too high. The minister must bear in mind that this perception is what really counts when we are trying to govern a country, and questions of immigration do, of course, bring out the whole problem of the integration and multicultural attitudes of our society.
It may seem strange, but the overwhelming proportion of people replying said that the manpower requirement was number one. Some people said that if we do not need the people to work here, they should not come in at all. It should not matter who they were related to, we should not let them come in at all. Ninety per cent of the respondents listed manpower requirements as the number one priority under which people should be allowed into the country.
The next item, of course, was the question of ethnic origin. That became rather an interesting situation. The question of ethnic origin came second and the question of humanitarian or family relationships came down low on the list, and that seems to be different from the attitudes which are expressed in the way things are happening. You ask these questions and then you begin to doubt the answers perhaps. You begin to say, well, you know, maybe the ministry knows best. But when you are looking at a question of immigration and you find that people are saying something dramatically different from what is really the practice or the happening in the Department of Employment and Immigration, you begin to wonder whether the department should not perhaps alter what it is doing.
Immigration Act
Earlier this session the Leader of the New Democratic Party asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) a question with respect to some pollings. It might well be appropriate for the minister to do some polling on attitudes with respect to immigration. The minister is continuing to get things like "Overview" from the National Citizens Coalition saying a number of rather tough things about the immigration program followed not only by this government but by the former government and by the government before that. It is not just the present minister who is getting it in the ear. The former minister of immigration got it in the ear from them, and I gather the present policy of the department, the way the minister is handling things, is essentially no different from the way the former minister was handling things. May I say the department is quite good at getting replies back to members of Parliament. I am quite pleased with the efficiency of the department. Perhaps there is an improvement in the efficiency. But the minister's approach is no different from that of his predecessor. Yet there is a lot of stir out there in the country on this matter. The coalition stirs it up. Undoubtedly the minister has been getting letters from a William Kelly, founding an organization known as Friends of the United Kingdom.
The minister knows that if we do not pay attention to the way people are reacting, we are going to have a very unhappy population. Surely to goodness it is the responsibility of his department to react and to run an immigration policy the way the people who are here as Canadian citizens want it run. It is not a question of some high faluting theory of people who are either far right or far left in their political ideology. It is a question of running immigration policy in accordance with the way the people who are in Canada right now seem to want it run. I therefore recommend to the minister that he do some private polling on this matter and perhaps make the attitudinal results available to members of Parliament.
My questionnaire went on to deal with attitudes with respect to the provision in the Immigration Act that five points are given if you decide to settle in an area of low unemployment. For example, as I said to a constituent on Saturday, "If your sister would only move to Calgary, I would bet she would find a job as a typist, and she would get in here instantly". That may be the case, but the situation is clear that there are extra points under the point system for where you happen to go in the country.
In an area like Mississauga the reply I get from 67 per cent of the people is that the minister should direct where immigrants go. He should make a form of contract with them, with some sort of a bonding system, and have people go to the north, to farms, and to certain places outside the great metropolitan areas. There may be a feeling that there are too many people in the cities and that the frontiers of the country should be expanded and developed. I do not know exactly where that feeling comes from, but I can say to the minister that enormous numbers of people replying convey that type of attitude. A typical reply is that simply giving an immigrant extra points to locate in a designated area does not accomplish

April 23, 1980
Immigration Act
the task because, if it takes extra points, all we have achieved is to admit an immigrant we do not really want in the area. If the immigrant is otherwise acceptable, he should not need extra points.
It is suggested that the government should facilitate viable settlements in the Yukon and Northwest Territories, for some reason, or the clay belt region.
I want to say to the minister that he should pay attention to these types of attitudes. The responses I am getting convey the attitude that there should be some direction to settle in a particular area, and that is with particular reference to the refugee program. There might be much more willingness to take more refugees if the refugees brought in were directed to certain specific outlying areas of the country as farm labour and so forth, and not allowed to come to the large cities.
The next question I raised was a question regarding appeal proceedings. The minister will remember that during the last election the former minister deported an East Indian lady after an alleged approximately $80,000 worth of expense. There is no question that that deportation was probably legally proper and all the rest of it, but the thing which bothered a great number of people-and it was brought to their attention-was the enormous amount of money which was expended on what people perceived to be a very extended appeal process. I want to tell the minister that some 65 per cent of the people responding indicated that they either wanted no appeal procedure at all or that the appeal procedure be a very brief and limited one, and directed only to one issue, whether the person is improperly or illegally in Canada, and no other issue, and they wanted no long string of appeals.
The other day there was a situation when I was involved with the minister where 1 suspect the minister issued a deportation order. The person being deported will appeal under the present law-quite properly, I think the minister will agree- and may well appeal right up to the Supreme Court of Canada. The question really boils down to whether Canada should finance a system of justice that allows persons who are not citizens, and who in many instances are illegally in the country or in the country only by permission, to use the court system, and the delay system that the court system we have in the act allows, to carry on with appeal after appeal and eventually use up, as was the case in the matter which came up during the election, some $80,000 in costs. That type of thing is just not acceptable to the vast majority of Canadians.
To summarize, I think there is a strong desire to see more strictness and some real selectivity, to make sure that manpower considerations are paramount and that when we bring in large numbers of people we have a policy which directs them more or less to new areas of the country so that we do not ghettoize people in the large cities. The interest of Canada in matters of immigration should come first.
1 commend the new minister on the taking over of his portfolio, and I wish him luck with that portfolio. It is a portfolio which causes great concern and heartache, and which sometimes is not too politically rewarding. I wish the minister well.
