Mr. Speaker, I support the minister's feeling, as he stated it today, that it is time we had a planned, rational refugee policy rather than the emotional ad hockery that seems to be fairly common in our non-policy and which tends to favour some refugees while ignoring others.
If anything, I think we need a fair, impartial, and planned refugee policy which considers international needs and which, of course, is based on Canada's ability to accommodate people. We need a refugee policy which is humanitarian and not political. Therefore I suggest that our policies should be seriously studied and redefined, and that we support United Nations refugee policies on a regular basis and not just react to emotional crises which arise from time to time, which often make us feel like short-term do-gooders but which really do not make much impact on the problems of this world.
I would like to mention just two or three examples which I think dramatized this during the period when I was the critic on immigration for the New Democratic Party. Last year Canada generously sponsored some 50,000 political refugees from southeast Asia. We speedily processed their applications. There was a minimum of delay. Yet, at the same time in Argentina when there was a desperate situation with political prisoners in jails-some of them were waiting in Brazil to get out of their first country of asylum-the Government of Canada promised one hundred visas. We ended up by taking only nine people, refugees from that country who arrived in Canada later. The people who tried to enter Canada from Brazil had to wait for at least six months because our processing was slow. The Brazilian government required, of course, that they leave before that time.
So it appears that we could speed up the processing when we want to, but perhaps at the expense of refugees in other parts of the world, in this case particularly in Latin America.
I should like to point out also the case of a young Chilian refugee, Galindo Madrid, well known in British Columbia. He jumped ship and came to Canada as a political refugee. It was later established by the UN authorities that he could not return to his country without facing injustices there. After two years in Canada, during which he worked as a dishwasher and proved himself to be a responsible person-dishwashing was probably the only job he could get-he was refused asylum in Canada from the very same government-at that time it was a Tory government-which went overboard with election emotionalism because when two young Russian lovers jumped ship in Vancouver, they were welcomed to Canada, in contrast to Galindo Madrid, and were given asylum immediately.
I mention these examples to illustrate the unfairness and the emotional and reactionary policy which we have at present, and I urge the new minister to be as open hearted in his approach to refugees from right wing regimes as he is to refugees from left wing regimes. 1 hope his criterion for admitting refugees will be humanitarianism, not political

April 23, 1980

prejudice. Of course we support the humanitarian needs of refugees who want to come to Canada at this time.
I should like to point out also that it is not good enough for us to consider only admission of refugees and immigrants without looking at what happens to them and what happens to Canadians, and looking at some of the feelings of Canadians once these immigrants and refugees come to Canada. It is very important that we have well planned immigrant services which will assist refugees and immigrants in general in adjusting quickly and in becoming established in Canada following their arrival. It is important that immigrant services be financed in a more flexible way-and 1 hope at some time to talk to the minister about this-and that these kinds of financial arrangements with immigrant service agencies be adopted in a flexible way over a three-year period at least.
As my colleague has mentioned, it takes longer than a three-year period for women to adjust. Immigrant women who come to Canada and who cannot speak English, who often raise children and cannot go out into the community as quickly as men, are now deprived of services if they have been here longer than three years. That means they will never adjust in this country, and that is why there are cases of grandmothers whose only contact is with their own family because they have been cut off from the Canadian community at large. That is another aspect we should consider.
Furthermore, there is a great need for the expansion of services for immigrant women who suffer double discrimination. If we look carefully and study the cases of immigrant women who are able to find jobs-many of them have to work in order to survive in Canada-we find them in jobs providing the lowest wages and very little in the way of benefits or protection. Often immigrant women are unable to obtain child care services, which prevents them from taking language classes. Often they are deprived of the possibility of participating in training programs, orientation programs and preemployment opportunities, all of which are important to their adjustment in Canada.
Our Immigration Act discriminates against immigrant women, treating them as spouses rather than as people with rights of their own as human beings.
1 think we should consider also the particular problems of immigrant workers who are working as domestics and farm workers, people who are brought to Canada because Canadians are not willing to do these jobs. These people have no rights when they come here, they have no benefits, and they are open to exploitation and intimidation by their employers. Domestic workers, many of whom are immigrant women in Canada, receive no UIC benefits, have no Canada Pension Plan, and are fearful of being deported if they complain about their work situation. They are unprotected by either federal or provincial labour legislation. Often they are overworked, having to work seven days a week, and underpaid. They have no recourse to appeal. I think the federal government should take leadership in developing policies and legislation to protect immigrant workers. After all, it is the federal government which brings them to Canada. It should prevent that kind of
Immigration Act
exploitation from taking place, rather than saying this comes under provincial jurisdiction.
It seems to me that if a domestic worker has worked for six months, or perhaps even longer, and has fulfilled the requirements, she should be entitled to receive landed immigrant status so she can have the protection that other workers have in Canada. The services of domestic workers are still needed here. So the federal government should take leadership in this area and not just leave it to the provinces to offer protection to immigrant workers whom we bring in to meet labour market demands in our country.
In British Columbia our farm workers, most of whom are of East Indian descent, have a terrible work situation. They receive low wages and are exploited by middle men who take their wages from them. They receive far below the minimum wage in many cases. Fortunately some of them are working for collective bargaining rights. This is something I would hope our government would support.
I know we are running short of time so I will be brief, but there is one very important and critical issue which I should like to raise at this time. It has to do with the current concern of many Canadians because of the infringement of human rights, and this could apply to either refugees, immigrants or Canadian-born citizens who are so-called visible minorities.
Our party, as I am sure are many members of the House, is seriously concerned at the repeated examples of racism and stereotyping which we have witnessed in the media in recent months, media that are supported by our tax dollars and are supposedly educating our citizens, and 1 shudder to think of the kind of education that some of these programs are giving to our children as well as to adults. Such programs inflame public prejudice and discrimination, attitudes that are only too prevalent among our citizens in times of economic stress.
Last year, a CBC program portrayed organized crime in such a way as to imply that most Italian Canadians have Mafia connections. At about the same time the National Film Board produced a very insensitive documentary on the Chinese community. It was produced largely in Vancouver. The misinformation and stereotyping in this film, which was called "Bamboo Lions and Dragons", was offensive not only to many Chinese people but to us non-Chinese who viewed it as well.
Most recently we had the incident of media misinformation and outright racism which was made public in the program called W5, entitled "Campus Giveaway". 1 hope that all hon. members are aware of the gross exaggeration in the stated number of foreign students in university programs, students who are not admitted unless there are spaces which are not required by Canadians. That program was a disservice to foreign students, and an insult to Canada's commitment to train young people for leadership roles in Third World countries. Much more serious, however, was the deliberate attempt to pick out and smear a group of Canadian students, probably many of them second or third generation Canadians of Asian descent. Because they were not Caucasian, Canadian-born citizens were accused of being foreigners with no right to a university education. In a country that stands proudly for

April 23, 1980
Immigration Act
multiculturalism, this is a national disgrace. It is not good enough, after denials over a seven-month period, that the CTV president apologized a few days ago. This was only two days before a national protest meeting was held.
I should like to quote one of the protestors who spoke at a meeting in Vancouver as follows:
The battle may be won but this does not remove the hurt.
An apology will not remove the insult and disrespect to thousands of Chinese Canadian citizens, nor will it assure that there will be no repetition of such incidents in the media. I am pleased that in this case an ongoing group has been formed called the "Chinese Canadian National Council for Equality". I know that this group plans to meet with other ethnic groups to form a strong coalition to do something about this discrimination and infringement of human rights. They are working to protect human rights for all and toward a true multicultural Canada. But this is not just the duty of those who are the victims of racist attitudes.
Those who are hurt should not be the only ones to object and have to defend themselves alone. Human rights are the responsibility of our country as a whole, and the responsibility of every citizen. Surely it is a particular responsibility of our media-the press, television, radio, columnists and film. Therefore I should like to present to the House and to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) several recommendations which were made at the meetings 1 attended in Vancouver.
First, media members should establish a code of conduct for their own industry and their own colleagues. Second, stronger legislation with teeth must be introduced to protect human rights and to be a deterrent to the kind of programming that we saw on W-5. Third, we should have a public ombudsman and positive programs on the media produced with advisory people from ethnic communities. Finally, members of Parliament must demand that there will be no more racist programs such as "Campus Giveaway" on Canadian television, particularly Canadian productions.
In the interest of time, I should just like to mention that there are a number of issues connected with the Immigration Act which very much require review and which I wish we had time to debate at this time. If we shorten our presentations, I would ask the minister if he would consider a time, perhaps during the hearings before the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration, when these issues could be discussed at some length.
Some of the aspects of the Immigration Act which I felt as immigration critic in the past really needed review were the following: the powers given to immigration agents to decide who is or is not desirable to come to Canada; appeal procedures, which certainly are very poor in regard to refugees but need improvement for other immigrants as well; discrimination against women immigrants, which I have already mentioned; policies which really disregard cultural differences, particularly the cultures of Asian countries where extended families are
considered to be families and where our policies tend to break up families. I know of many cases-and I am sure other members do as well-where children as they turn 21 must be left in their home country while their parents come to this country. This is quite unacceptable to many immigrants from India and from Hong Kong. We give special concessions to entrepreneurs and to people with capital, yet we make it very difficult for many other immigrants to come to Canada.
Of course our immigration policy must take first account of the concerns of Canadians. We must have jobs and housing for all. In times of economic stress, in many ways it is understandable that people who are finding it hard to find jobs, to find a house or shelter for themselves and their children, are resentful of newcomers who seem to find homes and jobs more easily. We know that it does not work that way. Immigrants create jobs. We are all immigrants. We must have positive programs to help create understanding. The best way to do this is to ensure that Canadians and immigrants alike have jobs, housing, and the services which they need in our communities.

Mr. Speaker, it is our ardent hope and desire, on this side of the House at least, to see Bill C-2 given second reading this afternoon. Therefore my remarks will be rather short.
In speaking in support of the bill, I should like to say that the concept which it embodies confirms that the immigrant in economic terms is a valuable asset to this country. There is a long-standing tradition to this effect. This is a program which started early in the 1950s. It is my understanding, as others have already said, that Canada has done this before then in order to attract people to this country.
It is a fact, although this belief is not shared by everybody in the country, that an adult immigrant arrives in this country as a productive individual. Having been raised at the expense of another jurisdiction, and being in good health at the expense of another jurisdiction, he becomes almost immediately upon arrival a participant in the community, not only as a consumer and producer but also as an active member of the community and therefore a highly valuable, positive asset in the community, centre, town, region, province, or nation as a whole. This is what Bill C-2 means to us. Evidentally all of us in this House support it. The amount reflects the fact that there are certain projects and programs which require more immediate support because of increasing costs in the world. It is a fact of life that we not only recognize but support.
However, this bill raises in the minds of those of us who are familiar with the pattern of immigration and settlement in Canada the fact that there is a weak link in the chain which is beyond the scope of this bill but is implicit in its wording. The weak link in the chain is the fact that in this country we have a service or network of so-called immigrant settlement and adaptation programs which are not adequate. In analysing this bill and in passing it, it is important that we make reference to the desirability of a successful adaptation of immigrants brought into the country under the auspices of the bill, in other
April 23, 1980

words, that we pay more attention to the needs of immigrants upon settlement.
The budget devoted to this particular program, the adaptation program, was in the neighbourhood of $2 million in the previous fiscal year. It runs in the same neighbourhood this fiscal year, with a slight decrease. I look at that fact in a very distressed manner. It seems to me that if we are embarking upon a program of this kind, we must increase the funding of this program, in particular the funding of volunteer agencies which are active in the communities across the country, mainly from Montreal to Vancouver, in facilitating the adaptation of the immigrants.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) made reference a moment ago to the three-year rule. I do not know whether the time frame is accurate, but whatever the time frame is, I would urge the government to reconsider it and to remove it entirely.
There are situations in which immigrants who arrive and settle never require services. There are cases and instances when services are required upon arrival, and there are in the last instance situations in which this need arises well after the so-called three-year rule. Therefore, the services ought to be made available in a flexible manner as the need arises and not with time limits imposed, of course, through bureaucratic criteria that really do not take into consideration the facts of life and the process of integration of the individual into the new community.
The next point I would like to make briefly has to do with the receiving society, Canadians born here and Canadian citizens by adoption, who see the arrival of new immigrants and who make the necessary adjustments in absorbing those new arrivals into the neighbourhoods and into the new communities.
Here again, as I understand it, the Secretary of State (Mr. Fox) has an important responsibility to perform in somehow facilitating and encouraging, on the part of the so-called host society, an attitude of understanding and adaptability so as to encourage and make the welcome of the newly arrived immigrant warmer and more cordial.
It is quite clear that this task again is one that needs to be urged upon the government through the facilities of the Secretary of State which, as I understand it, is the department that keeps the pulse of Canadian society as a dynamic entity, in continuous change and in continuous adaptation as a result of the constant yearly immigration of individuals from various continents who come to settle in this country.
In order to make Bill C-2 effective, and in order to make the process of the adaptation of new immigrants in years to come not only easier but more successful, there are two ingredients required; one is a stronger immigrant settlement and adaptation program, and the second has to do with the preparation of the host society so as to be better equipped in receiving the newly arrived individuals.
Immigration Act
Before I sit down, I would like in my intervention to reply briefly to a suggestion made earlier by the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) who, in his long deliberation, which actually deserves perhaps the yearly top award to the politician who most successfully manages to talk out of both sides of his mouth, made one point clearly. He recommended that immigrants be sent to specific destinations for employment purposes, and that they be, if I understood him clearly, destined to such places for a certain period of time.
We on this side of the House reject this notion because it would create in Canada two classes of individuals, those who are free to move and those who are not. That is unacceptable. The strength of Canada's immigration policy has been that as a nation Canada has achieved something rather unique, namely, that it has treated and continues to treat immigrants, except for the right of voting, in the same manner as those who were born here and who are Canadian citizens. In humanistic terms that is a very rare and highly commendable achievement. We do not want to have this record spoiled by a suggestion of the kind made by the hon. member for Mississauga South.
Finally, if ever the Canadian government were to adopt a measure like this it would contravene both the spirit and the letter of the Helsinki Agreement which we signed in 1975, and which contains as a very strong premise the freedom of movement within countries and between countries. We would like to see that respected and implemented by other countries around the world as well.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 do want to make a short contribution to this debate, and I hope it will be a contribution.
Most blanket policies have severe weaknesses, and I would endeavour to prove this afternoon to the hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), particularly, if he indeed requires that proof, that blanket policies of the Department of Employment and Immigration also have very severe weaknesses.
Let us take as an example the view of many people in Canada who say we should not bring immigrants in because we have 900,000 or one million people unemployed. That has a very severe weakness. It may well be sound that we should not bring immigrants in who are going to be in heavily unemployed areas where there is much unskilled labour. It is totally in error when we suggest that we should not bring unskilled labour into other parts of the country.
I want to point out two or three places in my own constituency of Bow River where there is a need for unskilled labour. When I receive letters from officials of the department of immigration refusing excellent applicants simply because they have not learned a trade or do not have a profession, I have difficulty explaining that to those people who want this type of worker.
For instance, let us consider our small towns, and 1 will use Bow River as an example. I suggest this would be applicable to

April 23, 1980
Immigration Act
almost any other rural riding in much of western Canada. There is no unemployment in our small towns and villages. The Canadian of Chinese origin who operates a restaurant in a small town many times works 14 hours a day while trying to raise his family, yet he cannot get help. It is useless for him to go to the manpower office in Calgary because most of the people will not go to a small town or village. As a result, the people in the small towns or villages have no one available.
When that Canadian of Chinese origin makes an application on behalf of a nephew or a niece in Hong Kong or mainland China who qualifies in every other way, I suggest it is not wrong to bring that person in even though he or she may be unskilled. I think that is in line with what the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery) was suggesting. These people are members of a family. This family will teach them the language, if that is required, and will make sure they continue to get their education, with the result that the Canadian of Chinese origin will not have to work 14 and 16 hours a day. That is the situation in many small towns, and 1 think it is applicable in many areas.
The next example I should like to give relates to farm work. There is an application before the department at the present time in respect of two young men from Bermuda who were met by the son of a farmer when he was there. They said they would like to come to Canada on a temporary basis to see what it was like, and work on a farm. This man has 2,000 turkeys arriving in a very few days and he cannot find anybody to help with the work. It requires a lot of work to care for 2,000 turkeys, and that is not particularly skilled work. The immigration officials interviewed one of these men-I have not heard about the second one-who was an hotel man, and they turned him down. That one man, at least, could have done that job on that turkey farm.
Many other farmers have been trying to obtain labour, but people will not come out and work on farms. There are many young men in Denmark, Sweden, Norway and countries like that, who would love to come and work in Canada. In many cases these are men of integrity but have no farming experience. In other cases these are men who were raised on a farm and who understand cattle and know the soil, the difference between loam and gumbo. Unfortunately many of these potential immigrants are turned down.
There are many farmers who are frustrated and discouraged because they cannot get help. The blanket policy of, "let's not bring people to Canada because we have unemployment", has several weaknesses with regard to small towns and our farms. There are many hon. members in this House who would agree that it is difficult to get certain types of labour in beautiful resort areas like Lake Louise and Banff. One of the motel operators in Lake Louise had to close early last year because he could not find workers. Lake Louise is not a large settlement of people from which to draw labour, and people will not come from Calgary. Here is a need for immigrants.
In referring to the situation in Lake Louise, I do not have particular types of immigrants in mind as I did in the other
two cases. Surely there are people in this world today who want to work at this type of job. I would like to see the minister put the boots to some of the people who hang around the unemployment office in Calgary and who will not go out on some of these jobs. The blanket policy is not sound, and I urge the minister to reject it and utilize a more flexible policy.
For example, if there is an unskilled member of a family who wishes to immigrate to a small town where his or her relatives are, then 1 think that we should have a policy to allow such a person to enter Canada. This person will become just as much a Canadian as his relatives have been, and I think that we can bring the right kind of people into the country in this way.
The other point I would like to make is with regard to the restaurant business in small towns. It is difficult to find Canadians who wish to do the menial tasks demanded by our society. Many immigrants would come to Canada and perform these menial tasks. They will take these jobs and try to work themselves up in society. So where Canadians are not available for these menial tasks, let us bring in immigrants who want to work. They can be of any colour or creed. 1 do not care whether they are black, yellow, pink, blue or white. The main thing is that they be people of high integrity, people who want to become Canadians and who will be loyal to this country.
The other point that 1 wish to mention is with regard to the refugee problem. I believe that we are our brother's keeper, and I think that it is a splendid thing that Canadians are prepared to take those who are suffering in other countries and who have no home and nothing to live for. I spoke to a recent refugee in Calgary, shortly before I returned to Ottawa. He spoke broken English, but 1 was amazed at his ability, for a man who had just come from a foreign country a few days before, at speaking English. He said, "Wonderful, wonderful; I have a job". The job was very menial, but he was happy that he had a job. He said in his broken English, "I love Canada". That man will become an excellent citizen. I think that we should encourage refugees to come to Canada. 1 have some people in my constituency who say we should not bring in too many. Perhaps we are bringing in a proper quota right now.
There are many Canadians who would like to better themselves through training in language and many other things, as do the refugees, and 1 hope that our policy is flexible enough to allow these Canadians the same advantages as the refugees, and thereby enable them to become good Canadians because, after all, charity begins at home.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in support of this bill. I want to remind the House that since the World War II, that is in the last 35 years, Canada has opened its doors to some 350,000 refugees. In other words, within the scope of our over-all immigration program, one immigrant in ten has come to Canada in that period, under the immigrant status. It also means that, in 35 years, 350,000 refugees have chosen to come to Canada,
350,000	new Canadians are Canadians by choice.
April 23, 1980

The importance of interest-free loans to allow the transportation of refugees cannot be doubted but it is important to point out to our people that after those refugees come to Canada, they have to reimburse the transportation costs. Generally speaking, Canadians think they pay to bring in the refugees to Canada, but the truth is totally different: the refugees reimburse their transportation costs at a later date.
Some of those who have benefited from that interest-free transportation loan later on expressed their gratituderconcrete-ly and in moving terms to the Canadians for the chance they have been given, through that free loan system, to start a new life in Canada, to find new hope and to prosper with their families in a free and welcoming land.
Throughout the years, several ethnic groups have benefited from those loans. For instance, the Hungarians, the Czechoslovaks, the Chileans, the Ugandans or, more recently, the Indo-Chinese. In truth, one of the main advantages of the loan system is that Canada can react more quickly to situations that are very complex and demand immediate action. It must be noted that, in this the twentieth century, in democracies such as the one in which we live, the main difficulty often lies in reaching a decision. To have substantial sums in readiness for interest-free loans gives the minister or Parliament the possibility of acting very rapidly and, as a first consequence, often those swift decisions allow us to bring people here fast, saving them from pressures or even simply from death, when the political or economic situation in the countries they must leave is critical.
The successive movements of refugees into Canada have proven clearly that each group could settle permanently in this country and contribute generously to the economic and cultural life in Canada. We all know, because we all have immigrants or refugees among our constituents, that those people have become full and active members of our communities.
My constituency of Manicouagan is 600 miles long by 1,250 miles wide and the co-operation and engineering competence of these refugees or immigrants has contributed greatly to the success of the important mining and hydroelectric projects that we have witnessed on the north shore in the last 20 years.
It can be said that those who came to the north shore to meet this challenge have been greatly appreciated, and this applies as much to the engineers as to the simple workers. As the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) said earlier, it is extremely important to realize that refugees and immigrants are a first-class work asset and wonderful even as simple citizens because they have chosen Canada while we have had the luck to be born here. These people make extraordinary efforts to come here and adapt to our country and they add a diversity to the Canadian community which can only enrich our nation.
I would like to take this opportunity to underline the very important work done by two mayors in my area, the mayor of Schefferville and the mayor of Sept-Iles, to help the Indo-
Immigration Act
Chinese refugees who had requested admission to Canada. The Manpower and Immigration employees in Sept-Iles also did an extraordinary job, and I would like the minister to take good notice of this fact because it is often said that public servants are too slow, that they are not really sensitive to the needs of the people. This afternoon, I want to emphasize that in our area, the reaction of the public servants to the plight of the Indo-Chinese refugees was marvellous and that the reception given to these people by the residents of Schefferville and Sept-Iles was extraordinary.
The bill now under consideration will enable Canada to maintain its considerable efforts to solve the problems of refugees throughout the world. Even though our attention has been focused mostly on the transfer of the Indo-Chinese refugees, which was probably the most important such operation ever undertaken in this country, the increase in the funds to be used for transport and which will be always available will enable Canada to pursue its humanitarian work in other parts of the world and allow us to receive in Canada, this land of freedom and prosperity, men and women seeking peace and justice.
I would also like to add that by opening our doors to refugees we seize the opportunity of having men and women who become the bulwarks of our rights and liberties. Often, these people have lived through extremely complex and difficult experiences in their country, which they must leave very quickly, and when they come here they enable us to detect in our system statutes or legislation which may constitute misuses of our rights and freedom. Often, as Canadians, we have never had the opportunity of expressing the fact that our rights and liberties are highly important values. These people make us realize that we can be proud of the level of freedom and rights that we enjoy, even though we may not be aware of it. These newcomers can make us realize this and by that token make us appreciate better our country.
As the minister said in his speech, this bill requires no financial commitment. But it is one step towards the creation of a world of sharing and openheartedness and I expect all members of this House to support the bill. I thank the minister for it and I hope we will grant it speedy passage.

It has to do with some of the non-North American diseases, or diseases that have been brought into the country that up to now have been unknown here. A fair number of them have been diagnosed and brought to the attention of hospital authorities. This is all the more worrisome for those who have these misgivings and concerns, and they are legitimate. A great number of these refugees have gone into the food-handling business.
Some of the diseases are transmittable by contact with the skin, by breath, and also, 1 believe, perspiratory glands. For example, there is a new type of flu that apparently has been introduced, also a new type of hepatitis which is most peculiar. Canadian dentists have been warned about this particular type of hepatitis. Hepatitis is a fairly disastrous type of disease. I had to spend about six weeks of my life recovering from it. 1 know that it is dangerous and that it comes from habits that we in Canada have managed to overcome, but this strain may well have been brought into this country by some of these refugees.
Tuberculosis has also been identified. I believe we had eliminated tuberculosis from the Canadian medical scene. Malaria is one of those extraordinary things that has cropped up. There may not be any anopheles mosquitoes in Canada. I hope that these types of mosquitoes were not brought in via luggage because malaria is a most debilitating disease. 1 was fortunate enough, though living in the tropics for many years, to have avoided that disease. However, I did see a number of people who suffered long-lasting disabilities because of the effects of malaria.
Then there is a form of gonorrhea that I believe is peculiar to Southeast Asia, which has been introduced into this country. I was assured by the authorities three or four months ago that proper medical attention was being paid to these people before they came into Canada.
I wonder whether the minister has had this matter brought to his attention and whether he feels that it is sufficiently worrisome to issue new instructions, or renew the instructions concerning medical examination of these refugees before they arrive in Canada.
1 hope there is no doubt in anyone's mind that these are cooked-up excuses by people who are unwilling or are resisting the introduction of these refugees from southeast Asia. I think it is worth noting that there have been alerts circulated to hospitals urging all medical personnel to make a note of any unusual diseases that cone to their attention, and to bring them to the attention of the provincial authorities. Furthermore, in the budget which was introduced in the legislature of British Columbia about two or three weeks ago, an additional $2.5 million was provided for the examination of the health of those refugees who are now in the country. It is not to check them as they come in because, and the minister should know this, it is assumed that there is a medical examination before they come.
True, they come from very desperate situations. That is understood. However, the fact remains that if there are illnesses or diseases, they should be diagnosed before the individuals arrive so that they can be properly treated once they arrive here. I did mention, and I think it is worth repeating, that some of these diseases of which I spoke are transferred by contact. Therefore the concentration of so many of these refugees in the food handling business has added to the concern of those who have expressed it to me.
Aside from that, there are a couple of matters 1 feel I would like to mention on this occasion. I doubt that there are many members in this House who have not had problems brought to them by persons from Britain seeking to emigrate to Canada to join members of their families. It may be a distant relative, an elderly sister or a married sister. This might be a widowed sister in Britain. I have in mind one such case.
There is another case where a person wanted to find out whether the social and physical climate was one to which he could accustom himself. He was very enterprising. He found a job. He found a prospective bride. That was fine. However, when the things were being processed, delays were encountered that would defy the imagination. The local immigration authorities would say, "It has just gone to Ottawa for processing, because we need this, that and the other thing." When it came back there would be another excuse. The bureaucratic excuses in this area of having British-born people emigrating from Britain into Canada have been a problem, and I would bet money on it, for every single member of this legislative body. I am sure everyone has had at least one case. 1 have had dozens of them.
All you have to do is try to emigrate from Britain and you are in trouble. I do not know why it should be, but it happens. Others come in. You would think there are the same rules, but I have had to write to the High Commissioner to have some matters looked into and have them put aside. I raise this, not because I want to but because it has been my experience. 1 do not get these problems with other countries, but I get them from Great Britain.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise to speak on Bill C-2, an amendment to the Immigration Act of 1976, whereby the amount of moneys will be raised from $20 million to $60 million. 1 wish to support this amendment, and at the same time offer a few thoughts about the question of immigration.
I would first like to extend to Madam Speaker my own personal congratulations on her new appointment. 1 remind the House that she is one of our native Saskatchewan daughters, having been born in Prud'homme, Saskatchewan. The people of her local community are extremely happy with the appointment.
I would also at this time extend my sincere congratulations to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy). It is my sincere hope that he will have the basic concern and sensitivity to what I consider to be a most difficult assignment, an assignment which will have an historical reality in the lives of millions of people in generations yet unborn, many times on his own personal decisions as to who will come and who will not come to our country.
During the last year Canada has responded to the needs of the "boat people" in what I believe was a very fitting and humane way. The "boat people" were special among immigrants because they received a very high media image. Television, radio, and other media coverage showed the unique way in which they escaped and became refugees. Millions of other people who are in a refugee state do not get the same kind of publicity, and therefore do not get the same kind of care. I believe that the "boat people" have already had a unique influence on Canadian life. I believe that Canadians, groups of
Immigration Act
them in communities or church groups, have responded to this new event in our history in a most generous and open way.
During the last week as I was visiting my constituency and other areas of western Canada, 1 met some of these new families, and I spoke to a number of Canadians who were sponsoring them. I can see a good overflow, a good interchange beginning to take place as prairie towns and villages have taken it upon themselves to integrate into their lives a family that a year ago they did not even know existed.
The "boat people" though, are only symbolic of what is taking place in the world as regards the migration populations. Never before in the history of the world has population pressure been at the intensity that it is in many sections of the planet at this time. Open lands and spaces are just not available as they once were even in our century. Today, millions upon millions of people are being pressed into situations of life which, because of lack of space, lack of food growing land, lack of places to live, have turned cities and other areas into great squalor and slums.
The social and political conditions which have brought this situation about cannot all be mentioned at this time, but the basic fact remains that millions in ever-increasing numbers are now living on the face of the earth in conditions which are not of a minimum human standard.
I say these things because 1 think that we, as Canadians, have been blessed in a most unbelievable way with great areas of land and possibilities and have to look seriously at a principle which states that "people without land have a right to land without people". Many, of course, can argue that this statement pertains to national lands, but as we enter this decade and the ones which are to come, I think we have less and less right to bar people from access to a better life because of the technicality of having been born in the wrong place. So I foresee in the future great migrations of people to land which is now vacant or, at least, underused, and this will come about either in a peaceful, bargained way, or it will come about by force. This is a principle that has descended through the ages of humankind. People without resources will finally take over the means they need for a better life.
To reflect on ourselves, I believe that most of the people sitting in this House are themselves immigrants, or else certainly the children of immigrants who came here within the last 372 years-excluding my hon. friend from the constituency of Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ittinuar) whose relatives arrived some
20,000	years earlier. In my own case, my family originated in Ireland and came here because of a population explosion and famine some 150 years ago. In the generations which have followed we have had the benefits which that first great tragedy brought indirectly through the migration of my ancestors.
My forefathers, like the forefathers of many other Canadians, were, of course, looked upon as strangers, as aliens, and there were prejudices against them when they came. Later on, they themselves developed prejudices against others who were

April 23, 1980
Immigration Act
either here before them or who came after them. The problem of having a prejudiced viewpoint remains true of everybody with human blood in their veins. It is a prejudice we have constantly to work against, particularly today when the peoples of the world, by circumstances and history, are forced to live outside their traditional, natural communities, and to mix as a planetary people. 1 believe the basic prejudices which people carry within themselves have had much to do with immigration laws and restrictions which, even today, work against certain groups who wish to enter into Canada.
1 trust the minister and his department will seriously take account at all times of laws which have built into them a prejudice against a certain type of person simply because such persons happen to be of a special colour or religion or political leaning, and will see that a bias of this kind is, as far as possible, eradicated from our immigration laws.
In just a moment I would like to speak about a particular instance which has come to my attention, having been raised by some of my constituents. It is an example of bias built in to our Canadian legal system. It specifically concerns Canadian families of Chinese origin who wish to bring in, from their former country, a relative who, according to Canadian standards, is not a relative because of differing marriage practices in China. In this particular case, a Chinese woman living in my constituency has been trying for a number of years to bring to Canada a man whom she considers to be her brother. However, in the Chinese tradition, her father had two wives. She belongs to the first wife and the brother belongs to the second. In these circumstances the brother has been refused entry. I hope that in future legislation we can be sensitive to the cultural norms of other peoples and respect them in bringing their families to our land, even though they may not truly fit the family standards which Canadian law lays down.
Finally, I would like to say that the immigration policies of Canada must be tied very closely to the whole of our foreign policy and that is why I believe there ought to be a complete revision and review of our foreign policy, tying it in very closely with the needs of populations around the world and how Canada will respond, not to the particular needs of Canada but to the particular needs of the planet.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few moments remaining I want to make a few remarks on Bill C-2. My hon. friends have expressed support for this bill and I think it will make Canada's welcome to immigrants much better than it was before.
As I sat listening to their remarks, I wanted to bring to the minister's attention a problem which the government's policies have created particularly for the city of Vancouver and, no doubt, for other regions where there are high immigrant levels. The problem is known by the call letters ESL, which stand for "English as a second language". It is one which has been created by the immigration policy of the federal government. It has been brought to the attention of both the federal minister and his predecessor by myself and, I am sure, by others.
We heard earlier about immigrants who do not learn the language, and we understand how that happens at times. The problem arises when children who speak no English attend Canadian schools. The total education program is, of course, delayed while the children are tutored in the English language, and the education of Canadian English-speaking children is held up while that process is taking place. The penalty falls upon those children whose education is delayed, and also upon the taxpayers of regions where immigration is high, because school boards are required to pick up the tab for this "English as a second language" instruction. In the case of Vancouver, the cost complained of by the school board amounts to something like $2 million a year. I just want that to be on the record. There is this problem, and the burden is a heavy one. It is an unfair situation, and the federal government owes it to the regional areas to come up with a solution.

Mr. Chairman, in the context of Bill C-2 and the whole question of immigrant assistance programs, I would like to raise a rather sensitive issue which leads to some questions which I would like to put to the minister while we have him present.
The matter relates to a quotation that has been brought to my attention in a recent issue of the Indo Canadian Times, published in Vancouver, and dated March 1, 1980. The front page of that issue shows a photograph of the present Prime Minister, and a translation of that article leads to some remarkable information which, to my surprise, never was put before the Canadian people during the recent election campaign. A partial transcript of that article, which is entitled "Efforts to free people who came to visit and gone underground", reads as follows:
Readers would remember that in the last issue at the time of the federal elections some prominent politicians stated that it is the policy of the Liberal Party to free (to grant landed immigrant status) to thousands of visitors who have gone underground, in case they get in power. Now the Liberal party is in power and we are going to form a committee who should take responsibility and in consultation with the heads of various organizations, take a deputation to Ottawa to meet the government and put pressure upon them to achieve this task by this summer.
The task, as rumored within the minister's own department, I understand, is to encourage the government to grant a general immigration amnesty, and to grant it by this summer.
I raise this at this time as a rather sensitive issue, and I hesitate to raise it because all of the speakers this afternoon, myself included, feel that we have much room in this country and much opportunity to continue to attract more and more

April 23, 1980

peoples from other parts of the world to enjoy the bountiful goodness of the Canada we know.
However, we have immigration laws in this country which demand respect. Our public servants are required to enforce these laws, and such a political promise or undertaking makes a travesty of those laws and, in fact, seriously complicates the whole question of all of the antagonisms which surround the immigration policies of our federal government. 1 do not at this time have the names of the prominent Liberal politicians, but I would be very anxious to hear the minister respond and indicate the extent to which he has knowledge of these undertakings, which were never discussed with the public but which, apparently, were used for the sole purpose of gathering votes, making a travesty of our immigration policy in the last general election.
Is the minister aware of an undertaking or a commitment to a general amnesty by certain Liberal politicians; who are these Liberal politicians; and is this not a flagrant abuse of innocent humans in encouraging them to come to this country illegally for the purpose of breaking an existing law which might be changed should a government be replaced?

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, 1 am somewhat taken aback by the questions raised by the hon. member because this is certainly the first that I have ever heard of any such suggestion or commitment. Frankly, I do not believe it. I have never heard anybody in our party state that there would be a general amnesty for any special group.
I recall-and this is simply from memory-that there was an amnesty declared several years back, prior to the passage of the Immigration Act, with respect to those who had been in the country for a long period of time, but that was a very clean cut period, and it came to an end.
1 can give the hon. member every assurance that there is no amnesty being planned, nor is there one in the planning process, nor is there one being contemplated. I have never heard any reference by anybody in our party or in my department to suggest that that was the case. I would be very pleased to receive from the hon. member a copy of the article to which he referred, to have it examined further and to see what the sources may be. 1 can give the hon. member the assurance, to ease his mind and the minds of others, that that is certainly not the case.
We do have an immigration law, and we are attempting to uphold it. As the hon. member well knows, with the large number of people coming to this country, enforcement is not always easy, but we do have a very effective enforcement branch. I heard in debate today from several other hon. members that some tend to think that our enforcement is too zealous at the present time and that we should, if hon. members will pardon the expression, liberalize it. At the same time, I would say that the amnesty question is something 1 would not want to contemplate, and we do not contemplate it.
As far as the other question about travel advertising is concerned, as the hon. member knows, that is not within the jurisdiction of my department, but I do believe-and this again is recalling from when I was sitting on the other side of the House-that there were some very strenuous attempts made by the previous government, as well as by the government previous to that, to encourage more visitors to Canada in order to provide some offset to the balance of payments losses that we have, and 1 suspect that there is a certain kind of ambition to bring more people to Canada to spend more

April 23, 1980
Immigration Act
money so that the money spent by tourists who leave Canada to go down south can be offset.
Again I assure the hon. member that there is certainly no illicit or ulterior motives behind that, other than to deal with the fiscal balance of payments problems. 1 will certainly take the matter up with the Minister of State (Trade) and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to ascertain what the advertising is, but 1 would say on the first hand that that would be the purpose of the advertising, not to do anything more than that.
As far as any other illicit purposes are concerned, one of the primary requirements under this act is to ensure that there is an impartiality in the application of the law. That is really the standard 1 intend to apply.
As the hon. member well knows, discretion has been exercised on a variety of grounds, and that is something that is treated with a great deal of care. Various ministers and governments have approached it with somewhat different philosophies, but that is a question of philosophy, not a question of any intention to break the law. It is simply a matter of applying different interpretations. Again I give him every assurance that in the enactment of this provision visas are not given out to visitors with a great deal of abandon. In fact they are given out very charily. As he knows, the changes to the Immigration Act in 1978 require any landed status to take place in a territory outside of Canada, which does provide a substantial check and balance against any abuse.
I think there should be some review. I have heard some very interesting and very helpful comments from members during this debate about how we might ensure that those laws do not abuse people or discriminate against them in reverse. I will take those under close recognition. I am very pleased to have those comments, but any other further purposes I would deny and simply say that we will enforce the law as it is written and try to provide the enforcement of that law with all the compassion we can bring to bear.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think it is necessary to extend the discussion much further because I can give every assurance to the hon. member that I took notice of his comments.
On the question of medical examination, anyone who applies to come into the country, whether through the normal route of immigration or by the special refugee program, is required to have medical examinations while outside the country. Usually they are given by Canadian doctors or people from the health services. Those are most rigorous and are applied to most tests. I am not sure that medical science is at a stage where it can detect all the exotic strains of viruses to which he referred, but I know that the kinds of medical examinations which are required are very, very rigorous. Also I can tell him that once refugees are landed in the staging areas in Canada, they are further subjected to additional medical examinations. In fact, when I visited the staging area at the Greaseback medical base outside of Edmonton, I witnessed the kind of medical review which is required of refugee families coming in there.
Also I should indicate to the hon. member that there is a high degree of consultation with the provincial health services because they have expressed these kinds of concerns. We have had several discussions with them, and they are prepared to provide special facilities or treatments when they are required. I would say to the hon. member it is not always the case that every refugee family or individual that we take is going to be totally able-bodied and totally well in all life and limb. Some of them suffer certain kinds of handicaps. As part of our refugee program, we think that we should have our fair share of those refugees who have those kinds of problems. Provincial health authorities have been most co-operative in ensuring that those kinds of facilities will be available. In fact in discussion with both the health minister in Ontario and the health minister in Alberta, it was indicated that they were prepared to take additional measures above and beyond the normal ones to ensure that there would be proper care facilities available for refugees who have special problems.
I would want to give the member every assurance that to the extent medical science offers us proper detection, we are
April 23, 1980

applying it. If there are further problems which he wants monitored, I will take it up with the department to see if there has been any evidence of anything special occurring. I would be quite glad to communicate that at a later date.

This could reach proportions which could be rather frightening. For example, internal parasites are something which I would like to think we have been free of in this country, but they could very easily spread with the type of work in which some of these people have been engaged.
I am glad of the assurances. I hope he will go on monitoring and making sure that there is this particular care in the medical health field for these people before they are admissible, and as they come in, to find if there are other diseases that were not detected during the initial investigation. I hope that the co-operation with the provinces will continue as he mentioned.
